messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null) is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.221.
\]

So the null‑hypothesis test’s standard deviation is roughly **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under null? Usually we compute standard error: sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null. That would be sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So about 0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard error is used. The test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic is 1? Actually the t distribution has variance n/(n-2) for df>2. But maybe they want the standard error.

Given the phrasing, likely they want the standard error: 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. So answer: approximately 0.221.

We can also compute the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test: maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null: same as standard error. So answer: 0.221.

Thus respond: The standard error is 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. If they want the standard deviation of the t distribution: sqrt(df/(df-2)) where df=39 gives sqrt(39/37) ≈ sqrt(1.054) ≈ 1.026. But likely not.

Thus answer: ~0.221.
